ACCEPTThe arbitrary- $r$  theorem is sound under the stated hypotheses. I found no geometric boundary failure, source-capacity failure, or reuse of an actual edge in the simultaneous completion. The argument establishes
$$\boxed{\min_{N\text{ full}} f(N)=\Lambda=\min_{1\le i\le r}\rho_i}$$
for every finite integer  $r\ge1$ , every unordered tuple of positive integer scales, every actual grid matching covering exactly the specified  $P$ , and every nonnegative real actual-edge weighting.Section 5 also correctly proves, for the canonical matching with unit weights,
$$f^*=\min_i k_i,
\qquad
\min_N C(N)=\sum_i k_i,
\qquad
f(N_C)=\sum_i k_i
\quad\text{for every }C\text{-minimizer }N_C.$$
I audited the supplied snapshot identified with commit 9968cd91d0826f131c7c1ee85ece2c1db2d9e8d1, starting with    STAIRCASE_HH_BUDGET_EXACTNESS.md, then   staircase_source_completion.py and   check_staircase_source_completion.py, together with the relevant imported definitions and predecessor arguments. This verdict is based on the present proof, not on the predecessor’s acceptance.Actual execution: the requested checker passed with assertions enabled. Its regenerated JSON equals the supplied original both structurally and byte for byte. Details appear below.1. Whole-exterior deletion lemmaThe partition and near-perfect matching are validThe identities
$$C_{i+1}=C_i+n_i,\qquad
R_{i+1}=R_i+n_i-2$$
are sufficient to justify the partition in §3. The completion blocks occupy disjoint, consecutive column intervals. Their row intervals overlap in exactly two rows, but that does not create shared vertices.Within column interval  $i$ , the upper rectangle, completion block, and lower rectangle exhaust the board. Their nonempty exterior heights are
$$\operatorname{height}(U_i)=4\sum_{a<i}k_a,
\qquad
\operatorname{height}(D_i)=4\sum_{a>i}k_a.$$
Thus every nonempty upper or lower rectangle has even height at least four and even width  $n_i$ . No ordering of the  $k_i$  is used.Each  $L_i$  has  $8k_i+3$  vertices, starts white, and alternates colours. For  $i<r$ , deleting  $z_i$ , at index  $4k_i$ , leaves segments of lengths
$$4k_i,\qquad 4k_i+2.$$
Both can be paired consecutively. Deleting the first white vertex from  $L_r$  likewise leaves an even path. Together with horizontal pairing of the upper and lower rectangles, this gives exactly
$$V(A)=O\setminus\{t_0\}.$$
In particular, every black vertex of  $O$  is matched by  $A$  to a selected white vertex. This matters later for the generic budget, not just for exterior completion.The rectangle connectivity claim survives unequal sizesThe contracted-pair argument in §3 is correct, although terse.Contract each horizontal  $A$ -pair to its white representative. Vertically adjacent pairs have directed connections in both directions, using the two different columns of the pairs. Horizontal connections between consecutive pairs point one way in one row and the opposite way in the next row. The bidirectional vertical connections therefore supply the missing horizontal direction. Every white vertex in a nonempty rectangle is mutually reachable with every other white vertex.For adjacent upper rectangles  $U_i,U_{i+1}$ , with  $2\le i<r$ , their common rows have height
$$R_i=4\sum_{a<i}k_a\ge4.$$
Across the shared column boundary, even and odd rows give opposite directed crossings. Thus the upper rectangles connect in both directions even when their heights differ greatly.For adjacent lower rectangles  $D_i,D_{i+1}$ , with  $1\le i<r-1$ , their common suffix has height
$$H-(R_{i+1}+n_{i+1})
=4\sum_{a>i+1}k_a\ge4.$$
Again, both row parities occur, giving both crossing directions.There is no hidden monotonicity assumption on the scales in either argument.All entrances, including their extreme coordinates, are legalThe alternating path along  $L_r$ , starting at its exposed first white vertex, reaches every white vertex of  $L_r$ . For  $r>1$ :The upward neighbour of  $t_0=(R_r,W-1)$  is a black vertex of  $U_r$ , whose  $A$ -mate is white in  $U_r$ .The leftward neighbour of the bottom-left white vertex  $(H-1,C_r)$  is a black vertex of  $D_{r-1}$ , whose  $A$ -mate is white there.These reach the entire upper and lower rectangle systems.The two entrance families into an earlier  $L_i$  also have the correct endpoint ranges:Target white vertex in  $L_i$ Incoming alternating routeBoundary check $(R_i+2j,C_i+n_i-1)$ ,  $0\le j\le2k_i-1$ White vertex in  $U_{i+1}$ , then the target’s black  $A$ -mate immediately below itThe entrance row is  $R_i+2j+1\le R_i+4k_i-1=R_{i+1}-1$ , so it remains in  $U_{i+1}$ . $(R_i+n_i-1,C_i+2j)$ ,  $0\le j\le2k_i$ White vertex in  $D_i$ , then the target’s black  $A$ -mate immediately to its rightThe entrance lies in row  $R_i+n_i$ , exactly the first row of  $D_i$ ; both extreme columns remain in its column interval.Thus the proof reaches every white vertex of  $O$ , including the whites closest to the deleted  $z_i$  and both ends of each bottom row.Only one exposure is needed for a constructed completion. Reachability of every possible target does not require simultaneously flipping all these routes: for the chosen target  $t$ , one simple alternating  $t_0$ -to- $t$  path suffices.The  $r=1$  endpoint is completeWhen  $r=1$ , there are no  $z_i$ , upper rectangles, or lower rectangles. The exterior is simply  $O=L_1$ . Pairing after exposing its first white vertex and following the alternating path reaches every white vertex. If the target is already  $t_0$ , no flip is needed.Accordingly, the whole-exterior deletion lemma holds at  $r=1$  without invoking any argument that requires another core.2. Relay existence and simultaneous physical completionThe pad argument works for every actual  $M_i$ The three required boundary deletions have explicit perfect matchings:Bottom midpoint: pair the first  $4k_i$  rows vertically; the two remaining bottom-row intervals each have length  $2k_i$ .Bottom-right corner: pair the first  $4k_i$  rows vertically and the even remainder of the bottom row horizontally.Top-left corner: pair the last  $4k_i$  rows vertically and the even remainder of the top row horizontally.After pairing the deleted boundary vertex with its exterior white pad, the auxiliary matching covers  $S_i\cup\{a\}$ . Its tagged union with arbitrary  $M_i$  has precisely  $h_i$  and  $a$  as degree-one vertices. Their component is therefore the required alternating path.The bottom-midpoint pad
$$t_i=(R_i+4k_i+1,\ C_i+2k_i)$$
lies inside the board, is white, and is distinct from every  $z_a$ . Hence  $t_i\in T$ . This proves finiteness of every  $\rho_i$ . The corner constructions supply the two adjacent-source possibilities wherever those sources exist.The internal  $\rho_i$  is also the relevant global feeThis identification is essential to the lower bound.In a tagged  $M\cup N$  decomposition, every  $Q$  vertex is an endpoint, so a terminal path cannot pass through a  $Q$  vertex internally. Moreover, different  $P_i$  have no adjacent vertices: even consecutive core squares have nearest columns differing by two.Consequently, a terminal path ending at  $h_i$  cannot travel through the exterior or another core before returning. Its interior lies in  $P_i$ . Thus a TH path to  $h_i$  has expense at least the internally defined  $\rho_i$ .All centres are black, while terminal paths have opposite-colour endpoints, so distinct centres belong to distinct paths. There are only  $r-1$  white HH sources. At least one centre is therefore TH, and nonnegativity gives
$$f(N)\ge\min_i\rho_i.$$
Any paid root admits a simultaneous completionFor an arbitrary chosen root  $j$ , the assignment
$$z_i\longmapsto
\begin{cases}
h_i,&i<j,\\
h_{i+1},&i\ge j
\end{cases}$$
uses every source once and assigns exactly one source to each nonroot core.Choose the resulting HH relay in each nonroot core and a shortest TH relay from some  $t\in T$  to  $h_j$ . The physical compatibility argument is valid:Relay interiors lie in distinct  $P_i$ .Their white endpoints are the distinct vertices  $z_1,\ldots,z_{r-1},t$ .Each relay uses complete actual pairs, so no unused actual edge has just one endpoint occupied by a relay.The relay auxiliary edges and doubled unused actual edges cover exactly
$$P\cup\{h_1,\ldots,h_r\}\cup Z\cup\{t\}.$$
The uncovered vertices are exactly  $O\setminus\{t\}$ , to which the exterior deletion lemma applies.No source, centre, actual edge, or auxiliary matching incidence is reused. The exterior matching consists of direct TH edges, so the resulting full matching satisfies
$$f(N_j)=\rho_j$$
for every chosen root  $j$ . Choosing a minimizing root establishes the claimed optimum.3. The generic source budget is exactly equal, including zero weightsSection 4 proves the weighted budget equality, rather than only the count that some centre must be TH.Let  $\ell_b$  be the globally shortest T-source expense at a black  $Q$  terminal. The preceding arguments give
$$\ell_b=
\begin{cases}
\rho_i,&b=h_i,\\
0,&b\in O_{\mathrm{black}}.
\end{cases}$$
The zero exterior fees follow from the direct T neighbours witnessed by  $A$ .For a white source  $z_i$ , its only first steps into  $P$  enter cores  $i$  and  $i+1$ . Its other first steps reach black  $Q$  sinks, where a directed route stops. Core separation prevents further cross-core travel. Both adjacent centres are reachable by the pad argument. Therefore its reachable centres are exactly
$$\{h_i,h_{i+1}\}.$$
With  $r-1$  capacity-one sources, a discount matching omits at least one centre. Hence
$$\Delta\le\sum_i\rho_i-\min_i\rho_i.$$
The assignment rooted at a minimizing  $j$  covers every other centre and attains this benefit. Thus
$$\Delta=\sum_i\rho_i-\min_i\rho_i,
\qquad
\Lambda=\sum_{b\in Q_{\mathrm{black}}}\ell_b-\Delta
=\min_i\rho_i.$$
This remains correct if some or all  $\rho_i$  vanish. The generic implementation may omit zero-benefit edges; removing those edges from the displayed assignment leaves its benefit unchanged. At  $r=1$ , the discount matching is empty and  $\Lambda=\rho_1$ .One nonblocking wording precision: §4 calls the centre incidence graph the “positive-benefit graph.” Literally, when some  $\rho_i=0$ , the positive-benefit graph is its restriction to positive-fee centres. The reachability graph still has the stated path incidence, and the equality argument and implementation handle zero fees correctly. This does not require a mathematical revision.4. Section 5: every canonical  $C$ -minimizer has the asserted feeThe conclusion uses the stated convention that  $C$  charges actual edges on all terminal paths, including HH paths; P-only cycles and doubled components contribute zero. Here the actual-edge weights are one.A terminal path containing  $q$  actual edges has length  $2q+1$ . For each centre:Centre’s terminal pathMinimum endpoint distanceMinimum actual-edge countTH $2k_i+1$ , since every selected source is outside  $S_i$  $k_i$ HH $4k_i+1$ , from either existing adjacent source  $z_{i-1}$  or  $z_i$  $2k_i$ The adjacent-source coordinates are
$$z_{i-1}=(R_i,C_i-1),\qquad
z_i=(R_i+4k_i,C_i+4k_i+1),$$
when the respective source exists. Both distance calculations are independent of neighbouring scales.Because distinct centres lie on distinct physical paths, the charges add:
$$C(N)\ge
\sum_i k_i+\sum_{\{i:h_i\text{ is HH}\}}k_i.$$
The canonical construction attains  $C=f=\sum_i k_i$ . Each straight bottom relay uses exactly  $k_i$  actual edges. Its source has index  $6k_i+2$  on  $L_i$ , whereas  $z_i$  has the earlier even index  $4k_i$ . The direct pairing of the prefix therefore pairs  $z_i$  to the next black vertex, giving zero actual expense on that HH component. The block completions and horizontal exterior pairings are disjoint.Since every  $k_i>0$ , a  $C$ -minimizer cannot have an HH centre. All centres are TH, giving
$$\sum_i k_i\le f(N_C)\le C(N_C)=\sum_i k_i.$$
This proves the assertion for every minimizer, including all tie-breaking choices.The numerical attainments are correctly restricted to canonical  $M$ . Arbitrary rematchings retain the geometric lower bounds but have exact values governed by  $\rho_i$ . Indeed, the executed single-core slices include rematchings whose relevant  $\rho_i$  rises from  $1$  to  $2$ .5. Implementation and complexityThe production solver supports the advertised
$$O(v\log v)\text{ arithmetic time},\qquad O(v)\text{ stored words},
\quad v=|V|.$$
The target-set construction is correctly included. In solve_staircase, each target set is formed by examining the at-most-four neighbours of each vertex in that core. Since the cores are disjoint, the total construction cost is
$$O\!\left(\sum_i|P_i|\right)=O(v).$$
It does not scan the entire board or all of  $T$  once per core.Each core receives one TH shortest-path search and at most one HH search. Their bounded-degree graphs have total size  $O(v)$ , so their combined Dijkstra cost is  $O(v\log v)$ . Exterior construction, one alternating BFS and flip, reconstruction, and the final linear physical decomposition remain within the stated bound.The inherited reversed Dijkstra routine also handles zero weights correctly. Its labels are lexicographic (expense, hops), so every step strictly increases the label even when its monetary cost is zero. This prevents a zero-cost predecessor cycle. A target terminal is detected before attempting to look up its actual mate.Two scope distinctions are correctly preserved:The executable accepts exact nonnegative integer weights; the mathematical proof permits nonnegative real weights.These are arithmetic-operation and stored-word bounds. Arbitrary-precision bit costs depend on weight size. The slower generic budget and brute-discount routines are checker computations, not part of the production complexity claim.6.
